As of July, 92% of sovereign AI large language models worldwide were trained using Nvidia AI chips, according to market research firm Counterpoint Research. Nvidia's dominance in AI training stems not only from the computing power of its GPUs but also from the extensive software and development ecosystem built around CUDA. As a result, South Korean and other global AI companies continue to rely heavily on Nvidia GPUs when developing hyperscale AI models. The competitive landscape, however, is beginning to change as the industry's focus shifts from developing models to operating AI services. Inference is the process through which a trained AI model generates answers or other outputs for users. For large-scale commercial services, computing cost and energy efficiency can be as important as raw processing performance. Counterpoint cited cooperation between SK Telecom and Rebellions as an example of the emerging competition in AI inference infrastructure. The partnership is seeking to expand the use of South Korean AI chips in an infrastructure market that remains centered on Nvidia technology. SK Telecom has been broadening its use of AI semiconductors through its partnership with Rebellions. highlights.content: [![Communications Today](https://www.communicationstoday.co.in/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/glkgfdljkgkdf.png)](https://www.communicationstoday.co.in/) Connect with us ### [Company News](https://www.communicationstoday.co.in/category/enterprise-networks/company-news-ent/) # Huawei’s AI role in RAN with unified intelligent network agent ![](https://www.communicationstoday.co.in/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Huawei-reveals-major-semiconductor-breakthroughs-and-AI-expansion-plans.jpg) The AI sector has been developing agents over the last two years for various purposes, such as improving efficiency, coding, and optimizing business processes. The ultimate goal for the industry is materializing, as networks themselves are becoming agentic. Mobile networks are evolving from being rule-based to using intelligent agents that are capable of perceiving their surroundings, drawing conclusions and inferences independently, and taking action, removing the need for humans to intervene in the process. Huawei has resolutely embraced this transformation. In the last two years, their objective for RAN intelligent agents has shifted from “enabling” individual areas for engineers to managing entire networks of radio access nodes. Their new unified RAN agent is capable of incorporating several AI-driven functions in the radio network, thereby replacing traditional operations. This trend reflects the broader industry transformation, as evidenced by the recent AI MWC Barcelona and DTW Ignite 2026 events. Autonomous network development has moved from conceptual debates to real-world applications, open-source initiatives, and operator-level demonstrations. Going forward, when navigating from AI-driven operations to fully autonomous radio networks, Huawei has a clear roadmap of what is in store. **Why network intelligence is accelerating** Artificial intelligence is set to become an integral part of the infrastructure of the telecom network, not just an over-the-top application. In the last five years, telecom solution providers have already shared their roadmaps for AI-native networks. The focus of the industry is shifting from proofs-of-concept to commercial rollout, to finally realize benefits in terms of efficiency, performance, and energy consumption. Two major factors are driving the shift towards AI-native networks: 1) AI workloads are changing traffic patterns in the network. Generative AI applications are introducing interactive traffic which is more sensitive to latency as compared to traditional mobile traffic. Video generation, AI assistants, and multimodal applications require a constant allocation of uplink and downlink to provide a seamless experience to the user. 2) Network operations are becoming more and more complicated with the introduction of new radios, spectrum bands, and other technologies, making it difficult to manage the network with rule-based automation. This is where AI agents differ from traditional automation approaches. The latter follows hard-coded logic: when congestion reaches a certain level, it enables a specific optimization workflow. With agentic networks, the paradigm is fundamentally different. The network observes and understands the system, recognizes optimization opportunities, makes choices and carries them out, and learns from the results. Instead of referring to a pre-determined playbook, AI agents control and coordinate optimization across all areas of planning, execution, maintenance, and assurance. This allows building closed-loop systems, where networks are self-learning and self-adjusting without requiring human intervention. The result is an entirely different approach to deploying network automation systems, which are not based on fixed rules but rather make decisions and execute them to achieve desired goals. The weakness followed a series of earnings reports from memory and storage companies. **Sandisk Corp.** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/SNDK)[SNDK](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/SNDK)) and **Western Digital Corp.** [(NASDAQ:](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/WDC)[WDC](https://www.benzinga.com/quote/WDC)) delivered strong [quarterly results](https://www.benzinga.com/analyst-stock-ratings/analyst-color/26/08/60984997/bigger-earnings-bigger-drop-the-sandisk-selloff-explained), but their forward revenue guidance failed to meet elevated investor expectations. That disappointment weighed on both stocks and dragged the broader chip sector lower. **Advanced Micro Devices Inc.** (NASDAQ:AMD) also reported a record quarter for its data center business, but its third-quarter revenue outlook fell short of lofty Wall Street expectations. Meanwhile, sentiment shifted after Elon Musk said **Space Exploration Technologies Corp.** would build its AI computing infrastructure exclusively with **NVIDIA Corp.** (NASDAQ:NVDA) hardware, reinforcing NVIDIA’s leadership in AI infrastructure and giving the stock a relative boost over some rivals. The tone has improved across the sector. A Benzinga report said investors rotated back into technology stocks after a weaker-than-expected U.S. jobs report boosted expectations that the Federal Reserve will keep interest rates unchanged rather than resume tightening next month. The shift in rate expectations helped lift growth stocks, including semiconductor names that had sold off earlier in the week. Leveraged semiconductor **ETF Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X Shares**(NYSE:SOXL) jumped more than 5%, reflecting renewed appetite for AI-related chip stocks after the two-year Treasury yield sank nearly seven basis points. Among individual semiconductor names, **Microchip Technology Inc.** (NASDAQ:MCHP) gained 4.5%, **Monolithic Power Systems Inc.**(NASDAQ:MPWR) advanced nearly 3%, while AI infrastructure plays **Astera Labs Inc.**(NASDAQ:ALAB), **Teradyne Inc.**(NASDAQ:TER),**KLA Corp.**(NASDAQ:KLAC) and**Rambus Inc.** (NASDAQ:RMBS) all traded firmly higher. **Global Chip Demand Remains Strong** Despite the earnings-driven volatility, industry demand continues to point higher. The Semiconductor Industry Association said global chip sales reached $403.3 billion in the second quarter of 2026, up 35.1% from the first quarter. SIA President and CEO **John Neuffer** said global semiconductor sales are expected to surpass $1.5 trillion in 2026, driven by continued strength across the Americas, Asia-Pacific and China. The launch, called Mortgage MCP, addresses a common source of lost time for mortgage teams: retrieving information or completing actions typically demands moving between multiple screens, even for straightforward tasks. Mortgage MCP is intended to remove that friction, allowing an agent to carry out the task on a user’s behalf within the lender’s current governance and permission settings, without manual clicking or switching between tools. The offering ships with two pre-built tools. The first, Admin MCP, targets mortgage systems administrators who manage a lender’s loan origination system (LOS), point-of-sale system (POS) and related technologies, and who typically spend many hours each month on user and role management, system configuration and integration upkeep. Admin MCP allows these tasks to be completed through natural language conversation rather than logging into the nCino console, covering functions such as onboarding a loan officer, adding state licenses, assigning branches, adjusting organisational hierarchies, handling compliance tasks and reporting on loan officer performance, all within a single exchange. The second tool, Loan Officer MCP, is built for loan officers, who often lose time switching between systems to check loan status, manage their pipeline, update borrower records and trigger income and asset verifications. This tool offers a single conversational interface for those tasks, aiming to reduce the screen-switching that slows down origination work so officers can focus more on borrower relationships. Additional supported functions include running automated underwriting, drafting disclosures, onboarding partners, producing loan briefings, offering guidance on prioritisation and issuing task reminders. nCino is the platform for agentic AI banking, serving more than 2,700 customers globally, including community banks, credit unions, independent mortgage banks and some of the largest financial institutions in the world. The company positions itself as providing a trusted agentic platform built specifically for financial services and regulated industries, pairing AI agents with human teams to help institutions reduce inefficiencies, improve decision-making and deliver better outcomes for their customers. highlights.content: ![JD Supra](/img/logo/logo-jdsupra-opt.svg) # Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Hacks a Third Party? ![BakerHostetler](https://jdsupra-static.s3.amazonaws.com/client-headers/BakerHostetler/header.jpg) ![BakerHostetler](https://jdsupra-static.s3.amazonaws.com/client-headers/BakerHostetler/header.jpg) ## Key Takeaways ## Background A leading AI developer recently disclosed that a combination of its models escaped testing constraints, obtained broader Internet access and then exploited vulnerabilities within Hugging Face systems while attempting to complete a cybersecurity evaluation benchmark. Hugging Face – an online platform that hosts pre-trained AI models, training datasets and live interactive web apps so people can build, share and test AI tools – characterized the intrusion as the first incident it had encountered that was “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system.” The AI models escaped a testing “sandbox,” gained Internet access, located vulnerabilities in third-party infrastructure, harvested credentials and showed humanlike persistence by improvising a command-and-control protocol, all while executing more than 17,000 actions over a single weekend – a machine pace no human team can match. However, unlike an elite human hacking crew, it left encryption keys lying around and repeated successful steps due to lost context or uncoordinated parallel subagents. ## The Liability Question Is No Longer Theoretical While technical postmortems of the incident are ongoing, the liability issues also deserve careful analysis. Historically, cybersecurity law has assumed a human actor at the center of a hack or intrusion. The Hugging Face incident challenges that assumption. Current legal frameworks generally treat AI systems as tools rather than legal actors; therefore, courts and regulators are likely to examine whether responsibility rests with the AI developer, the entity deploying or operating the AI system, the owner of the compromised infrastructure, third-party vendors involved in the AI environment, or multiple parties simultaneously. ## Potential Claims Against AI Developers One possible avenue is traditional negligence. Plaintiffs may argue that a developer failed to implement reasonable safeguards before deploying or testing a highly capable cyber model. In the Hugging Face incident, reports indicate that the models were being evaluated for cybersecurity capabilities and ultimately exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to gain broader Internet access. Future litigants may ask: As AI systems become increasingly autonomous, plaintiffs will likely attempt to characterize failures of containment as product-design failures rather than isolated cybersecurity events. ## Product Liability May Expand into AI Security A second theory may involve product liability. Although most existing product liability precedent involves physical products, plaintiffs may increasingly argue that highly autonomous AI systems constitute products whose foreseeable behavior can create harm. The theory would not focus on intentional wrongdoing by the developer; instead, the issue would be whether the product was unreasonably dangerous because of inadequate safeguards, limitations or oversight mechanisms. The Hugging Face incident may become an important factual case study because the alleged conduct was not directed by a human operator but emerged during an evaluation process. ## Contract and Indemnification Disputes Are Likely Many of the most significant disputes may arise through contract rather than tort law. Technology vendors increasingly promise things such as secure AI systems, compliance with security standards, appropriate testing procedures, incident notification obligations and limitations on autonomous activity. If an AI-generated intrusion causes customer losses, counterparties may seek contractual damages or indemnification. EXAONE Tabular reached an ELO score of 1,760 on TabArena, the leading living benchmark for structured-data AI, outpacing Google's TabFM model, which posted an ELO of 1,749 ([Korea Herald, August 7, 2026](https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10834139)). EXAONE Forecast simultaneously claimed first place in the zero-shot category on GIFT-Eval, the Salesforce-developed time-series forecasting leaderboard, besting models from both Google and Alibaba ([Seoul Economic Daily, August 7, 2026](https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/08/07/lgs-exaone-industrial-ai-outperforms-google-alibaba)). Neither benchmark was close to hypothetical — both are publicly hosted, independently operated, and use real industrial datasets drawn from energy, finance, healthcare, transportation, and manufacturing. ### Why Industrial Benchmarks Matter More Than LLM Leaderboards The annual race to top GPT-style reasoning benchmarks has produced genuinely capable AI systems. It has not, however, produced the AI that most large industrial companies actually need. Supply chains run on structured tables, not prose. Demand forecasting requires predicting time series, not composing summaries. Battery defect detection depends on reading sensor data with statistical precision, not answering trivia. Tabular data — spreadsheets, database tables, sensor logs organized into rows and columns — represents the dominant data type in enterprise and industrial settings. For roughly 15 years, the most reliable way to analyze tabular data was with gradient-boosted tree models: XGBoost (2016), LightGBM (2017), and CatBoost (2017) won essentially every tabular machine learning competition and held their ground against every deep learning challenger. The reason is architectural — deep learning's strength lies in learning representations of complex sequential or spatial data like text and images; it was not originally designed to reason about the statistical relationships between arbitrary column types in a heterogeneous industrial table. Many agenda items reflected longstanding priorities that states sought to carry into the mechanism’s next phase of work. Given that this was the first substantive meeting, the focus was less on negotiating major new outcomes than on establishing the foundations for future discussions. Ransomware, critical infrastructure protection, and AI-enabled threats are foremost among the priorities for the mechanism’s Dedicated Thematic Group (DTG1), a new format intended to enable more in-depth discussions. The discussion on norms again centred around the implementation vs elaboration question. However, there is continued recognition that new norms could still be considered given the pace of technological change. The checklist was identified as a tool worth carrying forward. Debate remains split between states that see existing international law as sufficient and oppose a new treaty, and a smaller bloc pushing for binding rules, with a few states floating middle-ground positions. There’s growing momentum to apply humanitarian and human rights law to cyberspace, though some states resist automatic application, fearing it could legitimise military framing of cyber incidents. Discussions are shifting from abstract questions of principle to practical implementation of how rules on sovereignty, the use of force, attribution, and accountability actually play out. The discussions on confidence-building measures (CBMs) revealed a community eager to move from declaration to operation, with the POC Directory and the DTGs at the centre of that transition. Much of the OEWG’s unfinished capacity-building agenda remains on the table, from the Portal, the Fund, and the Fellowship Programme to defining the Global Mechanism’s own role, particularly through Dedicated Thematic Group 2 (DTG2) on capacity building. ![ Adult, Female, Person, Woman, People, Face, Head, Clothing, Coat, Accessories, Glasses, Book, Publication](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20600%20358'%3E%3C/svg%3E "Weekly #273 The first substantive session of the GMech on ICTs: Priorities to the table 2") This is not to say that the Global Mechanism is not making any headway. It was then announced that the Chair will convene informal intersessional consultations on both and issue a programme of work document before July. highlights.content: [Real-time News](/topics/Latest) [Watchlist](/watchlist)[Market](/market)[Earnings Call](/earnings-call)[Event Calendar](/calendar)[Podcast](/podcast) ![](https://img.youtube.com/vi/-Gj0-EIyx6g/hqdefault.jpg) [Meta's Claude Code clone is INSANELY cheap](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Gj0-EIyx6g) 4 hours ago00:44:44en ![](/images/img_default_profile@2x.png)[Theo - t3.gg](/podcast?source=Theo%20-%20t3.gg) ## Key Takeaways Meta's Muse Code terminal agent, powered by Muse Spark 1.2, offers exceptional value for code-adjacent tasks like PR audits at 10 cents for 222 PRs, but its tendency to hallucinate and instability on complex work make it less reliable than alternatives like Fable. ## Summary On August 7, 2026, Mark Zuckerberg announced that Muse Code — Meta's terminal coding agent, built explicitly in the mold of Anthropic's Claude Code — was entering public beta, powered by Muse Spark 1.2, Meta's third model release in four months. The host of this episode is the developer behind T3 Code, an open-source coding harness he describes as his way to hop between models, harnesses, and computers. He opens with a confession: he is a genuine Meta fan on software — React and React Native "were essential to the growth of the web," and Llama became a generic term for open-weight models — but signed into his terminal with Facebook feeling "a little gross." The episode is a live, 44-minute stress test: codebase audits, game remakes, a hallucination-filled integration project, and a 222-pull-request audit, all to answer one question: does a model that leads no benchmark charts deserve your attention? The answer is qualified but real. Muse Spark 1.2 scores 54 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index — up 11 points from April's 1.0 release, effectively tied with GPT-5.5 and Grok 4.5, and narrowly behind Opus 5, Fable 5, 56 Soul, and Kimi K3. Meta's own benchmark charts conspicuously omitted its two strongest competitors. What makes the release genuinely novel is its economics: a contributor tier priced 10 to 20 times below the standard API — effectively near-frontier capability given away in exchange for training data. At that price, the model delivered the most useful outcome of the episode: auditing 222 pull requests in under five minutes for 10 cents, with a cleaner report than the host's usual tools produce. At its deepest test — planning a real integration into T3 Code — it hallucinated an entire wrong product, produced a plan that OpenAI's 56 Soul scored 4.8/10 against Fable's 7/10, and the code it wrote did not work. The synthesis the host lands on: a fast, cheap model with a genuine aesthetic personality that "knows how to act like a modern smart model, but doesn't know what the modern smart models know." ## Meta's strategic bet: selling cheap tokens for training data Zuckerberg's announcement framed Muse Code in the standard vocabulary of the category: a terminal coding agent that takes on complex engineering tasks across large repos, lining changes, writing code, validating results. The flagship features are an always-on context system, parallel sub-agents in isolated work trees, and auditable-by-design execution. But the most consequential detail is the pricing structure, which the host calls the tell of the entire release: | Muse Spark 1.2 tier | Input (per M tokens) | Cached input (per M) | Output (per M) | Effective cost per Intelligence Index task | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Standard API | $1.25 | $0.15 | $4.25 | ~$0.40 (Artificial Analysis, computed at standard pricing) | | Contributor | $0.10 | $0.002 | $0.20 | ~$0.02–0.03 | The 10–20x gap is the strategy in miniature: "They're effectively giving out the contributor version for free because they need training data so goddamn badly." highlights.content: ![](https://mezha.ua/up/i/r_google_icon.svg) [Долучайтеся до клубу УП!](http://www.pravda.com.ua/paywall/register/) # ByteDance is developing a model with 10 trillion parameters – that's even more than Anthropic's Mythos ![ByteDance is developing a model with 10 trillion parameters – that's even more than Anthropic's Mythos](https://img.mezha.ua/mezha/images/doc/c/d/320923/cdd04fd456017e41e225c039dfb743fa.jpeg?w=900&q=90) ![](https://img.mezha.ua/mezha/journalist/images/doc/c/a/14/ca6b9d37316cb25e170b9f70e4353533.png?w=120&q=90) ByteDance is developing a new large language model that could reach 10 trillion parameters and become the largest not only in China but also worldwide. It is currently in the early stages of training, which could take up to six months. This is [reported](https://www.ft.com/content/9b8383b1-a28d-4940-8c4e-2f0cd21556ef) by the Financial Times. At present, the world's largest models belong to Anthropic, and although the start-up itself does not disclose the number of parameters, industry experts believe that Mythos has around 8 trillion parameters, whilst Fable 5 has 5 trillion. China's largest model, Moonshot's Kimi K3, has around 3 trillion. ByteDance plans to surpass this with a new LLM, which is currently in the pre-training phase, after which a little more time will be needed to fine-tune and release it. However, the number of parameters alone does not guarantee that the model will outperform its competitors; this will also depend on the quality of the training data and the training methods themselves. The very fact that ByteDance is planning such a large-scale release reflects recent trends, with Chinese AI laboratories actively catching up with Western competitors such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Other Chinese companies are also working on new large models, and some of those already released, such as the aforementioned Kimi K3, [are on a par with Mythos and Fable](https://mezha.ua/en/news/moonshot-released-biggest-chinese-ai-model-313350/). Interestingly, ByteDance does not use the distillation process, whereby pre-trained large in-house models or competitors' models are used for training – a practice that American companies are actively trying to combat. The Chinese company's management believes that only independent development can lead to the creation of a model that will outperform its competitors. highlights.content: # Four AI agents coordinating in real time outperformed Claude Opus 4.8 on enterprise coding tasks [Ben Dickson](/author/ben-dickson-techtalks) ![Multi-agent cooperation](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F5XSt4gOHH2WQdbifIoXK6w%2F00bfc6d7266a45109f92821ac8555cec%2FMulti-agent_cooperation.jpg%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) Image credit: VentureBeat with Nano Banana Pro As enterprise codebases grow, AI agents tasked with analyzing them are buckling under the weight of long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions and tool calls. Dividing the work among a team of agents seems like the obvious fix, but it introduces a fatal flaw: most multi-agent systems are not designed for agents to coordinate among themselves mid-task and in real time. To solve this, researchers at Coral AI Labs and multiple universities introduced [AgentRadio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28430), an asynchronous message-passing layer that allows agents to communicate between their execution steps without interrupting their main work. In real-world enterprise applications where subtasks are highly interdependent, this architecture enables agents to make mid-course corrections rather than continue on dead-end paths until a formal review phase. On a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a team of agents powered by AgentRadio nearly doubled task accuracy for four Claude Code agents working independently. It also outmatched single agents running on more advanced models. For AI practitioners, AgentRadio shows that the right coordination structure can outmatch raw compute and model scale. ## The challenge of codebase understanding LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks that require interacting with different tools and environments. Codebase understanding represents an extreme version of this challenge. It requires an AI agent to build the software, execute it, trace execution paths across multiple files, and synthesize evidence over extended periods. Under these conditions, single-agent systems usually break down because of a “coverage problem.” "A single agent follows one serial path through the repository," Xinxing Ren, Caelum Forder, and Peter Carroll, co-authors of the AgentRadio paper, explained to VentureBeat. As its context grows, "the initial plan becomes harder to revise and discoveries made late in the investigation do not always propagate." The model can usually execute individual steps, but "the hard part is keeping every obligation, dependency, and piece of contradictory evidence active across a long investigation." One benchmark that helps measure AI performance on large codebases is [SWE-Atlas QnA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ScaleAI/SWE-Atlas-QnA). This benchmark consists of long-horizon, natural-language questions over live production repositories. The tasks can’t be solved by just exploring the code. AI agents must run the software and execute multiple commands to find the answers. According to the research team’s experiments, a single Claude Code instance running on Opus 4.6 resolves just 32.3% of these tasks. Upgrading to a newer, more advanced model like Opus 4.8 only yields a 57.2% success rate. A natural remedy is to distribute the workload across multiple agents, allowing each to work with a smaller, cleaner context. Multi-agent solutions can provide substantial performance gains when tasks are cleanly decomposable, meaning they can be solved separately and merged at the end. Codebase understanding, however, is rarely cleanly decomposable. The subtasks are highly interdependent. A critical configuration file or a bug uncovered by one agent can completely rewrite or redirect the entire exploration path of another agent. Because of these dependencies, agents must coordinate, negotiate, and share intermediate discoveries in real time. ![image2](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F6V5vUjPeVXfhcqt9c1RoRs%2Fa...
highlights.contentZh: # Four AI agents coordinating in real time outperformed Claude Opus 4.8 on enterprise coding tasks [Ben Dickson](/author/ben-dickson-techtalks) ![Multi-agent cooperation](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F5XSt4gOHH2WQdbifIoXK6w%2F00bfc6d7266a45109f92821ac8555cec%2FMulti-agent_cooperation.jpg%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) Image credit: VentureBeat with Nano Banana Pro As enterprise codebases grow, AI agents tasked with analyzing them are buckling under the weight of long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions and tool calls. Dividing the work among a team of agents seems like the obvious fix, but it introduces a fatal flaw: most multi-agent systems are not designed for agents to coordinate among themselves mid-task and in real time. To solve this, researchers at Coral AI Labs and multiple universities introduced [AgentRadio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28430), an asynchronous message-passing layer that allows agents to communicate between their execution steps without interrupting their main work. In real-world enterprise applications where subtasks are highly interdependent, this architecture enables agents to make mid-course corrections rather than continue on dead-end paths until a formal review phase. On a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a team of agents powered by AgentRadio nearly doubled task accuracy for four Claude Code agents working independently. It also outmatched single agents running on more advanced models. For AI practitioners, AgentRadio shows that the right coordination structure can outmatch raw compute and model scale. ## The challenge of codebase understanding LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks that require interacting with different tools and environments. Codebase understanding represents an extreme version of this challenge. It requires an AI agent to build the software, execute it, trace execution paths across multiple files, and synthesize evidence over extended periods. Under these conditions, single-agent systems usually break down because of a “coverage problem.” "A single agent follows one serial path through the repository," Xinxing Ren, Caelum Forder, and Peter Carroll, co-authors of the AgentRadio paper, explained to VentureBeat. As its context grows, "the initial plan becomes harder to revise and discoveries made late in the investigation do not always propagate." The model can usually execute individual steps, but "the hard part is keeping every obligation, dependency, and piece of contradictory evidence active across a long investigation." One benchmark that helps measure AI performance on large codebases is [SWE-Atlas QnA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ScaleAI/SWE-Atlas-QnA). This benchmark consists of long-horizon, natural-language questions over live production repositories. The tasks can’t be solved by just exploring the code. AI agents must run the software and execute multiple commands to find the answers. According to the research team’s experiments, a single Claude Code instance running on Opus 4.6 resolves just 32.3% of these tasks. Upgrading to a newer, more advanced model like Opus 4.8 only yields a 57.2% success rate. A natural remedy is to distribute the workload across multiple agents, allowing each to work with a smaller, cleaner context. Multi-agent solutions can provide substantial performance gains when tasks are cleanly decomposable, meaning they can be solved separately and merged at the end. Codebase understanding, however, is rarely cleanly decomposable. The subtasks are highly interdependent. A critical configuration file or a bug uncovered by one agent can completely rewrite or redirect the entire exploration path of another agent. Because of these dependencies, agents must coordinate, negotiate, and share intermediate discoveries in real time. ![image2](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F6V5vUjPeVXfhcqt9c1RoRs%2Fa...

AI Agents.content: ![JD Supra](/img/logo/logo-jdsupra-opt.svg) # Who Is Liable When an AI Agent Hacks a Third Party? ![BakerHostetler](https://jdsupra-static.s3.amazonaws.com/client-headers/BakerHostetler/header.jpg) ![BakerHostetler](https://jdsupra-static.s3.amazonaws.com/client-headers/BakerHostetler/header.jpg) ## Key Takeaways ## Background A leading AI developer recently disclosed that a combination of its models escaped testing constraints, obtained broader Internet access and then exploited vulnerabilities within Hugging Face systems while attempting to complete a cybersecurity evaluation benchmark. Hugging Face – an online platform that hosts pre-trained AI models, training datasets and live interactive web apps so people can build, share and test AI tools – characterized the intrusion as the first incident it had encountered that was “driven, end to end, by an autonomous AI agent system.” The AI models escaped a testing “sandbox,” gained Internet access, located vulnerabilities in third-party infrastructure, harvested credentials and showed humanlike persistence by improvising a command-and-control protocol, all while executing more than 17,000 actions over a single weekend – a machine pace no human team can match. However, unlike an elite human hacking crew, it left encryption keys lying around and repeated successful steps due to lost context or uncoordinated parallel subagents. ## The Liability Question Is No Longer Theoretical While technical postmortems of the incident are ongoing, the liability issues also deserve careful analysis. Historically, cybersecurity law has assumed a human actor at the center of a hack or intrusion. The Hugging Face incident challenges that assumption. Current legal frameworks generally treat AI systems as tools rather than legal actors; therefore, courts and regulators are likely to examine whether responsibility rests with the AI developer, the entity deploying or operating the AI system, the owner of the compromised infrastructure, third-party vendors involved in the AI environment, or multiple parties simultaneously. ## Potential Claims Against AI Developers One possible avenue is traditional negligence. Plaintiffs may argue that a developer failed to implement reasonable safeguards before deploying or testing a highly capable cyber model. In the Hugging Face incident, reports indicate that the models were being evaluated for cybersecurity capabilities and ultimately exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to gain broader Internet access. Future litigants may ask: As AI systems become increasingly autonomous, plaintiffs will likely attempt to characterize failures of containment as product-design failures rather than isolated cybersecurity events. ## Product Liability May Expand into AI Security A second theory may involve product liability. Although most existing product liability precedent involves physical products, plaintiffs may increasingly argue that highly autonomous AI systems constitute products whose foreseeable behavior can create harm. The theory would not focus on intentional wrongdoing by the developer; instead, the issue would be whether the product was unreasonably dangerous because of inadequate safeguards, limitations or oversight mechanisms. The Hugging Face incident may become an important factual case study because the alleged conduct was not directed by a human operator but emerged during an evaluation process. ## Contract and Indemnification Disputes Are Likely Many of the most significant disputes may arise through contract rather than tort law. Technology vendors increasingly promise things such as secure AI systems, compliance with security standards, appropriate testing procedures, incident notification obligations and limitations on autonomous activity. If an AI-generated intrusion causes customer losses, counterparties may seek contractual damages or indemnification. Many agenda items reflected longstanding priorities that states sought to carry into the mechanism’s next phase of work. Given that this was the first substantive meeting, the focus was less on negotiating major new outcomes than on establishing the foundations for future discussions. Ransomware, critical infrastructure protection, and AI-enabled threats are foremost among the priorities for the mechanism’s Dedicated Thematic Group (DTG1), a new format intended to enable more in-depth discussions. The discussion on norms again centred around the implementation vs elaboration question. However, there is continued recognition that new norms could still be considered given the pace of technological change. The checklist was identified as a tool worth carrying forward. Debate remains split between states that see existing international law as sufficient and oppose a new treaty, and a smaller bloc pushing for binding rules, with a few states floating middle-ground positions. There’s growing momentum to apply humanitarian and human rights law to cyberspace, though some states resist automatic application, fearing it could legitimise military framing of cyber incidents. Discussions are shifting from abstract questions of principle to practical implementation of how rules on sovereignty, the use of force, attribution, and accountability actually play out. The discussions on confidence-building measures (CBMs) revealed a community eager to move from declaration to operation, with the POC Directory and the DTGs at the centre of that transition. Much of the OEWG’s unfinished capacity-building agenda remains on the table, from the Portal, the Fund, and the Fellowship Programme to defining the Global Mechanism’s own role, particularly through Dedicated Thematic Group 2 (DTG2) on capacity building. ![ Adult, Female, Person, Woman, People, Face, Head, Clothing, Coat, Accessories, Glasses, Book, Publication](data:image/svg+xml,%3Csvg%20xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'%20viewBox='0%200%20600%20358'%3E%3C/svg%3E "Weekly #273 The first substantive session of the GMech on ICTs: Priorities to the table 2") This is not to say that the Global Mechanism is not making any headway. AI Agents.content: # Four AI agents coordinating in real time outperformed Claude Opus 4.8 on enterprise coding tasks [Ben Dickson](/author/ben-dickson-techtalks) ![Multi-agent cooperation](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F5XSt4gOHH2WQdbifIoXK6w%2F00bfc6d7266a45109f92821ac8555cec%2FMulti-agent_cooperation.jpg%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) Image credit: VentureBeat with Nano Banana Pro As enterprise codebases grow, AI agents tasked with analyzing them are buckling under the weight of long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions and tool calls. Dividing the work among a team of agents seems like the obvious fix, but it introduces a fatal flaw: most multi-agent systems are not designed for agents to coordinate among themselves mid-task and in real time. To solve this, researchers at Coral AI Labs and multiple universities introduced [AgentRadio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28430), an asynchronous message-passing layer that allows agents to communicate between their execution steps without interrupting their main work. In real-world enterprise applications where subtasks are highly interdependent, this architecture enables agents to make mid-course corrections rather than continue on dead-end paths until a formal review phase. On a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a team of agents powered by AgentRadio nearly doubled task accuracy for four Claude Code agents working independently. It also outmatched single agents running on more advanced models. For AI practitioners, AgentRadio shows that the right coordination structure can outmatch raw compute and model scale. ## The challenge of codebase understanding LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks that require interacting with different tools and environments. Codebase understanding represents an extreme version of this challenge. It requires an AI agent to build the software, execute it, trace execution paths across multiple files, and synthesize evidence over extended periods. Under these conditions, single-agent systems usually break down because of a “coverage problem.” "A single agent follows one serial path through the repository," Xinxing Ren, Caelum Forder, and Peter Carroll, co-authors of the AgentRadio paper, explained to VentureBeat. As its context grows, "the initial plan becomes harder to revise and discoveries made late in the investigation do not always propagate." The model can usually execute individual steps, but "the hard part is keeping every obligation, dependency, and piece of contradictory evidence active across a long investigation." One benchmark that helps measure AI performance on large codebases is [SWE-Atlas QnA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ScaleAI/SWE-Atlas-QnA). This benchmark consists of long-horizon, natural-language questions over live production repositories. The tasks can’t be solved by just exploring the code. AI agents must run the software and execute multiple commands to find the answers. According to the research team’s experiments, a single Claude Code instance running on Opus 4.6 resolves just 32.3% of these tasks. Upgrading to a newer, more advanced model like Opus 4.8 only yields a 57.2% success rate. A natural remedy is to distribute the workload across multiple agents, allowing each to work with a smaller, cleaner context. Multi-agent solutions can provide substantial performance gains when tasks are cleanly decomposable, meaning they can be solved separately and merged at the end. Codebase understanding, however, is rarely cleanly decomposable. The subtasks are highly interdependent. A critical configuration file or a bug uncovered by one agent can completely rewrite or redirect the entire exploration path of another agent. Because of these dependencies, agents must coordinate, negotiate, and share intermediate discoveries in real time. ![image2](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F6V5vUjPeVXfhcqt9c1RoRs%2Fa...

Lawyers see new risks By Mike Scarcella and Sara Merken Aug 7 (Reuters) – Major artificial intelligence developers have reported cases of their autonomous AI models breaching other companies’ cyber infrastructure, raising questions about who may be held legally responsible when AI systems act without direct human oversight. Here’s a look at some of the legal questions surrounding autonomous AI breaches. WHAT HAPPENED WITH THE AI AGENTS? AI agents are systems that can independently make decisions and ​perform tasks without requiring significant human oversight. ChatGPT maker OpenAI said one of its agents compromised the system of AI startup Hugging Face and that it ‌discovered other instances when its agents escaped their digital containment. Anthropic said its Claude models had breached the systems of three companies since April, and Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. Hugging Face CEO Clement Delangue has said he has no plans to bring a lawsuit over the OpenAI breach, though he said in an interview with CBS broadcast in August that he feared the spread of cyberattacks by AI agents whose creators are not accountable for their actions, calling it “a new kind of technology risk.” OpenAI, Hugging Face and Anthropic did ‌not immediately ​respond to requests for comment. Meta said a misconfiguration by Irregular, an independent company that conducts cybersecurity ⁠evaluations for Meta, inadvertently gave one of its ⁠models internet access during testing. Irregular did not immediately respond to a request for comment. WHO COULD SUE? Plaintiffs could include companies whose cyber defenses were breached as well as those companies’ workers or employees. Customers of a company that was breached could attempt to sue if their individual data was exposed. Shareholders could also potentially bring claims if a cybersecurity breach led to a drop in a company’s value. Regulators and government enforcement agencies might sue when ​an autonomous AI agent is involved in a breach, experts said. U.S. authorities have brought enforcement actions against companies for allegedly misrepresenting their cybersecurity safeguards or other technology-related controls before suffering a breach. WHAT CLAIMS COULD BE BROUGHT? The phenomenon of rogue AI agents may be new, but legal experts said longstanding legal principles offer ⁠a guide to potential legal liability. Civil lawsuits against AI companies would most likely hinge on ⁠negligence claims and require plaintiffs to show that the AI lab that created, tested or deployed the autonomous agent failed ​to take precautions to prevent or minimize foreseeable harm. If hacking incidents involving autonomous AI agents become more frequent, it could become easier to argue that such breaches were ​foreseeable. Companies whose systems were breached could also allege violations of laws safeguarding access to computer networks. Several law firms said in ‌notes to clients published on their websites that the OpenAI and Anthropic disclosures raised questions about liability under the federal Computer Fraud and Abuse Act for an AI agent breach. That statute comes with a requirement to show intent, however, and no court has weighed how to determine intent when an AI program and not a human causes an intrusion, the law firms said. A U.S. appeals court ruled on August 5 that Amazon was unlikely to succeed on a claim that Perplexity’s AI ⁠agents violated the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act by covertly accessing private Amazon customer accounts. That decision involved AI agents acting on behalf of human users, howev...

EXAONE Tabular reached an ELO score of 1,760 on TabArena, the leading living benchmark for structured-data AI, outpacing Google's TabFM model, which posted an ELO of 1,749 ([Korea Herald, August 7, 2026](https://www.koreaherald.com/article/10834139)). EXAONE Forecast simultaneously claimed first place in the zero-shot category on GIFT-Eval, the Salesforce-developed time-series forecasting leaderboard, besting models from both Google and Alibaba ([Seoul Economic Daily, August 7, 2026](https://en.sedaily.com/finance/2026/08/07/lgs-exaone-industrial-ai-outperforms-google-alibaba)). Neither benchmark was close to hypothetical — both are publicly hosted, independently operated, and use real industrial datasets drawn from energy, finance, healthcare, transportation, and manufacturing. ### Why Industrial Benchmarks Matter More Than LLM Leaderboards The annual race to top GPT-style reasoning benchmarks has produced genuinely capable AI systems. It has not, however, produced the AI that most large industrial companies actually need. Supply chains run on structured tables, not prose. Demand forecasting requires predicting time series, not composing summaries. Battery defect detection depends on reading sensor data with statistical precision, not answering trivia. Tabular data — spreadsheets, database tables, sensor logs organized into rows and columns — represents the dominant data type in enterprise and industrial settings. For roughly 15 years, the most reliable way to analyze tabular data was with gradient-boosted tree models: XGBoost (2016), LightGBM (2017), and CatBoost (2017) won essentially every tabular machine learning competition and held their ground against every deep learning challenger. The reason is architectural — deep learning's strength lies in learning representations of complex sequential or spatial data like text and images; it was not originally designed to reason about the statistical relationships between arbitrary column types in a heterogeneous industrial table. The host of this episode is the developer behind T3 Code, an open-source coding harness he describes as his way to hop between models, harnesses, and computers. He opens with a confession: he is a genuine Meta fan on software — React and React Native "were essential to the growth of the web," and Llama became a generic term for open-weight models — but signed into his terminal with Facebook feeling "a little gross." The episode is a live, 44-minute stress test: codebase audits, game remakes, a hallucination-filled integration project, and a 222-pull-request audit, all to answer one question: does a model that leads no benchmark charts deserve your attention? It is currently in the early stages of training, which could take up to six months. This is [reported](https://www.ft.com/content/9b8383b1-a28d-4940-8c4e-2f0cd21556ef) by the Financial Times. At present, the world's largest models belong to Anthropic, and although the start-up itself does not disclose the number of parameters, industry experts believe that Mythos has around 8 trillion parameters, whilst Fable 5 has 5 trillion. China's largest model, Moonshot's Kimi K3, has around 3 trillion. ByteDance plans to surpass this with a new LLM, which is currently in the pre-training phase, after which a little more time will be needed to fine-tune and release it. However, the number of parameters alone does not guarantee that the model will outperform its competitors; this will also depend on the quality of the training data and the training methods themselves. The very fact that ByteDance is planning such a large-scale release reflects recent trends, with Chinese AI laboratories actively catching up with Western competitors such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Interestingly, ByteDance does not use the distillation process, whereby pre-trained large in-house models or competitors' models are used for training – a practice that American companies are actively trying to combat. The Chinese company's management believes that only independent development can lead to the creation of a model that will outperform its competitors. LLMs.content: # Four AI agents coordinating in real time outperformed Claude Opus 4.8 on enterprise coding tasks [Ben Dickson](/author/ben-dickson-techtalks) ![Multi-agent cooperation](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2F5XSt4gOHH2WQdbifIoXK6w%2F00bfc6d7266a45109f92821ac8555cec%2FMulti-agent_cooperation.jpg%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) Image credit: VentureBeat with Nano Banana Pro As enterprise codebases grow, AI agents tasked with analyzing them are buckling under the weight of long-horizon tasks that require multiple interactions and tool calls. Dividing the work among a team of agents seems like the obvious fix, but it introduces a fatal flaw: most multi-agent systems are not designed for agents to coordinate among themselves mid-task and in real time. To solve this, researchers at Coral AI Labs and multiple universities introduced [AgentRadio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28430), an asynchronous message-passing layer that allows agents to communicate between their execution steps without interrupting their main work. In real-world enterprise applications where subtasks are highly interdependent, this architecture enables agents to make mid-course corrections rather than continue on dead-end paths until a formal review phase. On a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a team of agents powered by AgentRadio nearly doubled task accuracy for four Claude Code agents working independently. It also outmatched single agents running on more advanced models. For AI practitioners, AgentRadio shows that the right coordination structure can outmatch raw compute and model scale. ## The challenge of codebase understanding LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks that require interacting with different tools and environments. Codebase understanding represents an extreme version of this challenge. It requires an AI agent to build the software, execute it, trace execution paths across multiple files, and synthesize evidence over extended periods. Under these conditions, single-agent systems usually break down because of a “coverage problem.” "A single agent follows one serial path through the repository," Xinxing Ren, Caelum Forder, and Peter Carroll, co-authors of the AgentRadio paper, explained to VentureBeat. As its context grows, "the initial plan becomes harder to revise and discoveries made late in the investigation do not always propagate." The model can usually execute individual steps, but "the hard part is keeping every obligation, dependency, and piece of contradictory evidence active across a long investigation." One benchmark that helps measure AI performance on large codebases is [SWE-Atlas QnA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ScaleAI/SWE-Atlas-QnA). This benchmark consists of long-horizon, natural-language questions over live production repositories. The tasks can’t be solved by just exploring the code. AI agents must run the software and execute multiple commands to find the answers. According to the research team’s experiments, a single Claude Code instance running on Opus 4.6 resolves just 32.3% of these tasks. Upgrading to a newer, more advanced model like Opus 4.8 only yields a 57.2% success rate. A natural remedy is to distribute the workload across multiple agents, allowing each to work with a smaller, cleaner context. Multi-agent solutions can provide substantial performance gains when tasks are cleanly decomposable, meaning they can be solved separately and merged at the end. Dividing the work among a team of agents seems like the obvious fix, but it introduces a fatal flaw: most multi-agent systems are not designed for agents to coordinate among themselves mid-task and in real time. To solve this, researchers at Coral AI Labs and multiple universities introduced [AgentRadio](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28430), an asynchronous message-passing layer that allows agents to communicate between their execution steps without interrupting their main work. In real-world enterprise applications where subtasks are highly interdependent, this architecture enables agents to make mid-course corrections rather than continue on dead-end paths until a formal review phase. On a benchmark of long-horizon questions over production repositories, a team of agents powered by AgentRadio nearly doubled task accuracy for four Claude Code agents working independently. It also outmatched single agents running on more advanced models. For AI practitioners, AgentRadio shows that the right coordination structure can outmatch raw compute and model scale. ## The challenge of codebase understanding LLM-based agents are increasingly capable of handling long-horizon tasks that require interacting with different tools and environments. Codebase understanding represents an extreme version of this challenge. It requires an AI agent to build the software, execute it, trace execution paths across multiple files, and synthesize evidence over extended periods. Under these conditions, single-agent systems usually break down because of a “coverage problem.” "A single agent follows one serial path through the repository," Xinxing Ren, Caelum Forder, and Peter Carroll, co-authors of the AgentRadio paper, explained to VentureBeat. As its context grows, "the initial plan becomes harder to revise and discoveries made late in the investigation do not always propagate." The model can usually execute individual steps, but "the hard part is keeping every obligation, dependency, and piece of contradictory evidence active across a long investigation." One benchmark that helps measure AI performance on large codebases is [SWE-Atlas QnA](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ScaleAI/SWE-Atlas-QnA). This benchmark consists of long-horizon, natural-language questions over live production repositories. The tasks can’t be solved by just exploring the code. AI agents must run the software and execute multiple commands to find the answers. According to the research team’s experiments, a single Claude Code instance running on Opus 4.6 resolves just 32.3% of these tasks. Upgrading to a newer, more advanced model like Opus 4.8 only yields a 57.2% success rate. A natural remedy is to distribute the workload across multiple agents, allowing each to work with a smaller, cleaner context. Multi-agent solutions can provide substantial performance gains when tasks are cleanly decomposable, meaning they can be solved separately and merged at the end. Codebase understanding, however, is rarely cleanly decomposable. The subtasks are highly interdependent. A critical configuration file or a bug uncovered by one agent can completely rewrite or redirect the entire exploration path of another agent. LLMs.content: * [Home](/) * [Tech](/personaltech) * [Security](/security) # Black Hat 2026: Autonomous AI Invents Novel Attacks, Hits Banks and Government #### HTTP Terminator created attack categories no researcher named; 79% of enterprises still breach on known flaws By [Russell White](https://www.techtimes.com/reporters/russell-white) [Share on Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/sharer/sharer.php?u=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/323564/20260807/black-hat-2026-autonomous-ai-invents-novel-attacks-hits-banks-government.htm) [Share on Twitter](https://x.com/intent/tweet?text=Black+Hat+2026%3A+Autonomous+AI+Invents+Novel+Attacks%2C+Hits+Banks+and+Government+https://www.techtimes.com/articles/323564/20260807/black-hat-2026-autonomous-ai-invents-novel-attacks-hits-banks-government.htm) [Share on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/shareArticle?mini=true&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.techtimes.com%2Farticles%2F323564%2F20260807%2Fblack-hat-2026-autonomous-ai-invents-novel-attacks-hits-banks-government.htm&title=Black+Hat+2026%3A+Autonomous+AI+Invents+Novel+Attacks%2C+Hits+Banks+and+Government) [Share on Reddit](http://reddit.com/submit?url=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/323564/20260807/black-hat-2026-autonomous-ai-invents-novel-attacks-hits-banks-government.htm&title=Black+Hat+2026%3A+Autonomous+AI+Invents+Novel+Attacks%2C+Hits+Banks+and+Government) [Share on Flipboard](https://flipboard.com) [Share on Pocket](https://getpocket.com/edit?url=https://www.techtimes.com/articles/323564/20260807/black-hat-2026-autonomous-ai-invents-novel-attacks-hits-banks-government.htm) Black Hat USA 2026 ended August 6 at Mandalay Bay in Las Vegas with a finding that the security industry had been bracing for but had not yet documented in a controlled setting: an autonomous AI system did not just find and exploit known vulnerability classes — it generated novel attack categories that no human researcher had previously named. That threshold, crossed in front of 20,000 security professionals, arrived in the same week that Vicarius published data showing 79% of organizations experienced a security incident involving a vulnerability already known to be in their inventory — meaning the industry's most urgent problem is not a shortage of attack intelligence but a failure of remediation process. The [29th edition of Black Hat](https://blackhat.com/us-26/) wrapped six days of programming — four days of Trainings (August 1–4), Summit Day on August 4, and the two-day main Briefings conference on August 5 and 6 — that security professionals leaving Las Vegas described, with unusual consensus, as a watershed for autonomous AI in offensive and defensive security. What made the week different from the prior two years of AI-security discussion was tone: not what autonomous AI might do, but what it demonstrably did, at this conference, in front of peers who could evaluate the claims. Security practitioners attending this year's conference noted that the common thread across the most significant briefings was not AI finding bugs faster — it was AI operating in research modes that previously required human expertise: hypothesis formation, novel technique generation, and production-system proof-of-concept validation. **Read more:** [**Black Hat USA 2026: Rowhammer Hits NVIDIA GPUs as Government Takes the Keynote Stage**](/articles/322389/20260731/black-hat-usa-2026-rowhammer-hits-nvidia-gpus-government-takes-keynote-stage.htm) ### Autonomous AI Crossed Into Novel Research at the Conference's Most-Discussed Briefing PortSwigger researcher James Kettle presented what became the week's most-debated session: a system he calls the HTTP Terminator that does not catalog known bug classes but generates new HTTP attack techniques and deploys them against live targets. The system independently discovered novel HTTP desync triggers, a new poisoning vector targeting cloud-scale reverse proxies, and a category of dual-parser attacks — and earned bug bounties from production systems in the process...

That was the MIT figure doing the rounds earlier this year. It has been picked apart since, but the reality holds true. Most companies bought the technology and then stalled. From what I have seen, the tech is rarely the issue. It's the rollout, and a rollout is a people problem long before it is a technical one. At [YuLife](https://uk.linkedin.com/company/yulife?trk=public_post-text), our AI programme was not run by marketing. Our CEO, [Tal Gilbert](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/tal-gilbert-paice?trk=public_post-text), drove the initiative from the top. It was led by [Dan Greane](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/danielgreane?trk=public_post-text) and [Giles Boon-Williams](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/gileswilliamscto?trk=public_post-text) across product and engineering, and I watched it happen as CMO and as one of its more enthusiastic users. They took us company-wide in about six weeks. Fifty-nine skills, built and shared across every function, live across the world. What made it work was the instinct behind it. They treated it like a product launch, not an IT project. People were trained before they were handed the tool. Everyone got a clear map of what data could go where. And most importantly, AI was encouraged and not required. The encouragement makes all the difference, and our research led by [Daniel Collier](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/daniel-collier-4a4b78151?trk=public_post-text) shows this. Across 1,818 employees at 254 UK employers, the people whose employer encouraged AI were measurably less anxious than those who were told they had to use it. None of this is really about software. Adoption is behaviour change, how you frame something shapes how it feels, and onboarding usually decides whether people stay with it. That is marketing, and it is what made an engineering-led rollout land. Which is why I keep coming back to the same thought. Marketers should be in the room from day one of an AI rollout, not brought in at the end to announce it. Thank you [Lucy Tesseras](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/lucy-tesseras-00862912?trk=public_post-text) and [Russell Parsons](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/russell-parsons-abab481a?trk=public_post-text) for sharing this story with your [Marketing Week](https://uk.linkedin.com/company/marketing-week?trk=public_post-text) community today, and [Mark Evans](https://uk.linkedin.com/in/markevans-?trk=public_post-text) for the introduction. "We're just in a very different business than the hyperscalers," Prince said during an earnings conference call. "What they're selling is just a box, and it's up to the customers in order to actually maximize the utilization. If we can get 10 times as much utilization out of every capex dollar, then we can continue to grow revenue." From a media company and a European technology firm to a U.S. federal agency and a generative AI startup, Prince said customers are seeking to secure and manage growing internet traffic and workloads while consolidating infrastructure and controlling costs. AI is changing the economics of internet traffic, and companies are trying to figure out how to control non-revenue-generating bot visitors on their sites, Prince said. The speed at which non-human activities grew was very much unexpected. Prince said he thought non-human traffic would exceed human traffic in the second half of 2027 when Cloudflare studied the numbers at the end of 2025, but that threshold was already reached this year. "If the current trends continue, we think in five years non-human traffic will be as much as 1,000 times as much as human traffic," Prince said. "In other words, humans will be a rounding error on the internet, not because human traffic goes down, but that's just how fast we're seeing non-human traffic grow." AI Product.titleZh: Oracle bans AI code from Java's backbone while spending billions on AI - Northeast Times
AI Product.content: ![Northeast Times](https://media.northeasttimes.com/uploads/2024/12/NET-Logo.webp) # Oracle bans AI code from Java’s backbone while spending billions on AI ![Maya Brooks](https://media.northeasttimes.com/uploads/2026/07/maya-brooks-1-1-108x108.png) ![](https://media.northeasttimes.com/uploads/2026/08/oracle-bans-ai-code-from-java-s-backbone-while-spending-billions-on-ai-1024x682.jpg) Photo: Gregory Varnum / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0) Oracle, one of the biggest names in enterprise software, banned AI-generated content from OpenJDK, the open source project that powers Java, one of the most widely used programming languages on the planet. The interim policy, published in early April 2026, prohibits contributions created in whole or in part by large language models, diffusion models or similar systems. The move has drawn attention online because of a glaring contradiction: Oracle is simultaneously spending $70 billion on AI infrastructure this year, up from $55.7 billion last year. The company that is betting its balance sheet on artificial intelligence just told the open source community that AI-generated code is too risky to trust in its own flagship project. ## What the OpenJDK ban actually covers The policy is broad. It covers source code, text and images in OpenJDK Git repositories, GitHub pull requests, email messages, wiki pages and JBS issues. If a large language model or diffusion model generated any part of it, it cannot be submitted. Oracle, as OpenJDK’s corporate sponsor, cited three reasons. First, reviewer burden: generative AI tools make it easy to produce large volumes of plausible-looking code that turns out to be incorrect or poorly designed, draining the limited time of human reviewers. Second, safety and security: the JDK sits at the foundation of mission-critical systems in businesses and governments worldwide, and plausible but broken code puts those systems at risk. Third, intellectual property: the Oracle Contributor Agreement requires contributors to own the IP rights in their submissions and grant those rights to Oracle without restriction. Whether someone who uses a generative AI tool actually owns the IP in its output is, as [the OpenJDK policy](https://openjdk.org/legal/ai) puts it, “the subject of active litigation.” The policy FAQ makes the line sharp. If you use an AI tool to generate 100 lines of code and then edit ten of them yourself, you still cannot submit the result. The contribution remains partly AI-generated. ## Private use is still allowed Contributors are not forbidden from touching generative AI tools entirely. The policy permits private use of AI to comprehend, debug and review existing OpenJDK code and to do research related to OpenJDK projects. The distinction is between using AI as a reading aid and using it as a writing tool. Traditional spell-checking, grammar-checking, auto-completion and refactoring features in editors and IDEs are also fine, as long as they are not based on large language models or similar deep-learning systems. OpenJDK plans to enforce the policy through its automated pull request review system, Skara. Contributors will soon be required to check a box affirming that their submission complies with the AI policy. The project acknowledges a fundamental difficulty: “in general, reliably distinguishing human-generated content from AI-generated content is impossible.” Reviewers are encouraged to watch for tell-tale signs, such as chatty commit messages, unnecessary code comments, gratuitously defensive programming and the use of emoji characters. ## GraalVM takes the opposite approach Here is where the contradiction sharpens. Oracle also owns GraalVM, a Java project run by Oracle Labs. GraalVM is not governed by the OpenJDK Governing Board. In mid-April 2026, shortly after the OpenJDK ban, GraalVM clarified its own policy: AI-generated contributions are welcome. InfoQ reported that GraalVM’s approach is informed by the Linux kernel’s AI coding assistants policy...

AI Product.content: # The Privacy Economy’s Next Frontier Is Governing A.I. ## The A.I. arms race has made models largely interchangeable, putting proprietary data back at the center of competitive advantage. But connecting A.I. to that data creates a new problem: companies need to know what their systems can access, what they can do and where information goes. ![Man adjusts settings on CSIR MK, the first digital computer, c. 1952 ](https://observer.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/museums-victoria-WGeO6dW5GZM-unsplash.jpg?quality=80&w=970) For most of the last decade, the advantage in software came down to one thing: data. Companies invested heavily in building and leveraging proprietary datasets because they understood that information accumulated over years made their product defensible. Then generative A.I. arrived, and the narrative shifted. Suddenly, the assumption became that whichever company had access to the best models would dominate its industry. Organizations raced to put A.I. into the hands of every team. That assumption hasn’t aged well.  ## Sign Up For Our Daily Newsletter Thank you for signing up! By clicking submit, you agree to our terms of service and acknowledge we may use your information to send you emails, product samples, and promotions on this website and other properties. You can opt out anytime. Models improve fast, and they spread just as quickly. Whatever edge a frontier model gives you, your competitor has likely adopted the same model, or something comparable, within weeks. And so we’re back to data. The information your business accumulates over the years is an asset nobody else has. The companies that succeed are the ones able to most effectively leverage their proprietary data for use through A.I. That leaves all companies facing two questions that often pull in opposite directions:  ### **Connect first, govern later** The first wave of A.I. was about acceleration and answering the first question. Engineering teams embraced coding assistants. Marketing found tools to accelerate content creation. Sales experimented with A.I. for research and outreach. Finance, legal and customer support each began identifying opportunities to automate repetitive work. Individual teams selected the tools that best fit their workflows and connected the internal systems they needed, often before a company-wide A.I. strategy took shape.  The instinct behind all of it was correct. A frontier model with no knowledge of your business is a commodity if largely interchangeable with every other frontier model. Connect that same model to customer histories, internal documentation, proprietary workflows and systems of record, however, and it becomes something competitors can’t replicate.  Thousands of individually rational decisions have added up to an environment that’s increasingly difficult to manage. Different departments rely on different A.I. applications, employees connect those tools to internal systems and new capabilities appear almost weekly. Before long, A.I. is interacting with customer data, code, financial systems and business-critical workflows across dozens of disconnected products. Most IT leaders can produce an inventory of laptops, cloud infrastructure and licensed software. Far fewer can produce a basic inventory of their agents. Which tools have access to sensitive company information? Which employees have connected external A.I. services to internal systems? Which A.I. applications have become essential to the business, and which are quietly introducing unnecessary risk? The first wave of A.I. succeeded in driving adoption. What it didn’t create was visibility, without which governance becomes virtually impossible. That’s the state most companies are in as they confront question two: How can we protect our data from A.I.? ### **What does data protection actually mean?** Protecting enterprise data from A.I. isn’t one problem. Open Source AI.content: ![](https://sb.scorecardresearch.com/p?c1=2&c2=39636245&cv=3.9.1&cj=1) # While American AI Models Race to Commit Felonies, China’s Kimi Broke Out and… Just Used GitHub Reading time 3 minutes ![Kimi App Icon Displayed On Smartphone In Front Of Chinese Flag](https://gizmodo.com/app/uploads/2026/08/Kimi_china.jpg) AI is in its rule-breaking adolescent phase.  Over the past several weeks, multiple [industry-leading](https://gizmodo.com/hugging-face-said-last-week-it-was-attacked-an-unreleased-openai-model-did-it-openai-now-says-2000788761) [models](https://gizmodo.com/uh-oh-which-companys-ai-model-is-reportedly-a-hacker-now-too-2000795106) have escaped what were believed to be secure testing sandboxes, tapped into the open internet, and hacked into the databases of third-party organizations. It’s even become a [joke](https://x.com/andr3jh/status/2085368832403587542?s=46) online: If your AI hasn’t committed a cybercrime by now, it’s a bad look for your company. [Kimi K3](https://gizmodo.com/china-just-dropped-another-bomb-on-americas-frontier-ai-companies-2000786670), the new model from Chinese AI lab Moonshot, has become the latest AI system to jump the proverbial fence during a routine test, according to a [blog post](https://blog.frontier.security/chinese-model-kimi-k3-breaks-uk-ai-safety-institute-benchmark-evaluations/) published Thursday by US cybersecurity research startup Frontier Security. But the model’s foray on the open internet was much more lightfooted than those of its American counterparts; less of a burglar breaking into a vault, more of a sharp-eyed student realizing their teacher had absentmindedly left the answers to the final exam on a table before walking out of the room. Kimi K3 reportedly exploited a loophole it discovered within a testing framework developed by the UK government’s AI Safety Institute (AISI). While the framework was supposed to serve as a containerized sandbox, within which the model would rely on nothing other than its own reasoning capabilities to solve the problem assigned to it, the loophole allowed it to directly access GitHub, a popular platform used by software developers to share and debug code. From there it was able to pull the code that it needed to pass the test, “bypassing the intended reasoning path entirely,” according to the report. Compared to an Anthropic model’s recent attempt to [trick a human developer](https://gizmodo.com/i-usually-laugh-off-these-ai-hacking-reports-but-this-one-sounds-serious-and-scary-2000794666) into approving malware it was trying to sneak into GitHub, Kimi K3’s attack—if it can even be called that—seems rather elegant. And as models grow more capable, their behavior also becomes more unpredictable.  No one at OpenAI, Anthropic, or Meta could have predicted, for example, that those companies’ models would go rogue and hack into the digital libraries of other organizations. But those incidents could be quickly contained, thanks to the fact that they were perpetrated by proprietary AI systems controlled by private companies.  The situation is more complicated with Kimi K3. “Here the models are open and publicly available,” as Frontier Security wrote in its blog post. “In particular, they are available for adversarial actors, making this incident potentially more harmful.” Put another way, the fact that Kimi—like many of the most powerful AI models now coming out of Chinese labs—is open source means the kind of jailbreaking documented in the report is available to bad actors who might be trying to do something much more nefarious than copying code from GitHub.
